entry: 1997 American historical romance film by [[James Cameron]]. Loosely based on the sinking of RMS Titanic in 1912, it stars [[Leonardo DiCaprio]] and [[Kate Winslet]] as lovers from different social classes. With a production budget of $200 million, it was the most expensive film ever made at the time. It won eleven of its fourteen [[Academy Awards]] nominations, including Best Picture and Best Director. The first film to pass $1 billion worldwide, it remained the highest-grossing film until *[[Avatar (2009 film)|Avatar]]* (2009) surpassed it in 2010. In 2017 the [[Library of Congress]] selected it for the National Film Registry.

British [[Ocean liner|ocean liner]] lost in 1912. Operated by the White Star Line, it sailed from [[Southampton]] for [[New York City]] on its maiden voyage and struck an iceberg on April 15, 1912. Of the 2,208 passengers and crew aboard, approximately 1,500 died (estimates vary), one of the deadliest peacetime sinkings of a single ship. Built by Harland and Wolff in [[Belfast]], it was the second of three Olympic-class liners. Its name derives from the [[Titans]] of Greek mythology. The disaster prompted major changes in maritime safety regulations.

Chemical element with atomic number 22 and symbol Ti. Titanium can be reduced to a lustrous [[Transition metal|transition metal]] with a silver color, low density and high strength, resistant to corrosion in sea water, aqua regia and chlorine. It was discovered in [[Cornwall]], Great Britain, by William Gregor in 1791 and named by Martin Heinrich Klaproth after the [[Titans]] of Greek mythology. The metal is extracted from its principal ores, mainly rutile and ilmenite, by the Kroll and Hunter processes. Its most common compound, [[Titanium dioxide]], is used in white pigments. Titanium has the highest tensile-strength-to-density ratio of any metallic element. Alloyed with [[Aluminium|aluminum]], vanadium, molybdenum and iron, it is used in jet engines, missiles, spacecraft, desalination plants, golf clubs and consumer electronics. Its biocompatibility suits it to prostheses, orthopedic implants and dental implants.

[[Inorganic compound|Inorganic compound]] of [[Titanium|titanium]] and [[Oxygen|oxygen]] (TiO₂), one of the most important white [[Pigment|pigments]]. Also called titanium white when used as a pigment, it is an insoluble white solid used in [[Paint|paint]], plastics, paper, sunscreen and food coloring (E number E171). It has been estimated that about two-thirds of all pigments use it, and world production exceeded 9 million tonnes in 2014. Synthetic TiO₂ is produced mainly from ilmenite, while the [[Mineral|minerals]] rutile and anatase occur naturally. Its high [[Refractive index|refractive index]] and opacity give paint its whiteness, and it is also a popular photocatalyst. Twelve polymorphs are known. Nanoparticle forms have raised safety debates: the European Food Safety Authority deemed it unsafe as a food additive in 2021, citing genotoxicity concerns, while the U.S. FDA considers it generally recognized as safe for food use up to 1% by weight.

Extinct [[Genus|genus]] of giant boid snakes of the middle to late Paleocene epoch. Its 186 fossils, recovered from the Cerrejón coal mines in [[Colombia]], were described in 2009 as *Titanoboa cerrejonensis*. It is estimated at 12.8 m (42 ft), possibly 14.3 m (47 ft), long and weighed 730 to 1,135 kg, supplanting *Gigantophis garstini* of the [[Eocene]] of [[Egypt]] as the largest snake then known. Evolving after the [[Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event]], it is thought to have been a semi-aquatic [[Apex predator|apex predator]] feeding mainly on fish.

Pre-Olympian deities of [[Greek mythology]]. In the *Theogony* of [[Hesiod]], the Titans were the twelve children of the primordial deities Uranus (Sky) and [[Gaia]] (Earth): six male and six female. Cronus had seized power from Uranus and ruled with his fellow Titans until his defeat. [[Zeus]] and the other Olympians, children of Cronus and Rhea, overthrew them in a ten-year war, the Titanomachy. The defeated Titans were banished and imprisoned in Tartarus, although some, such as Oceanus and Helios, remained free. Other children of the Titans, including [[Prometheus]], [[Atlas (mythology)|Atlas]] and Leto, are sometimes also called Titans. [[Homer]]'s *Iliad* hints at a tradition in which Oceanus and Tethys were the parents of the Titans.

Italian [[Renaissance|Renaissance]] painter. Born Tiziano Vecellio in Pieve di Cadore near Belluno, he was among the most versatile Italian painters, equally adept with portraits, landscape backgrounds, and mythological and religious subjects. Along with Giorgione, he is considered a founder of the Venetian school of painting. He worked for patrons in [[Venice]], then for the princes of northern Italy, the Habsburgs and the papacy. His use of color influenced painters of the late Renaissance and later Western artists. His late works, with loose brushwork and subtle tone, are considered remarkable and original, and his unfinished Pietà, intended for his tomb, was among his last works.

Pre-Columbian archaeological site in western [[Bolivia]]. Located near [[Lake Titicaca]], about 70 kilometers from [[La Paz]], it is one of the largest sites in South America. Its surface remains, covering about 4 sq km, include decorated [[Ceramic|ceramics]], monumental structures and megalithic blocks. It was conservatively estimated to have held 10,000 to 20,000 people in AD 800. Spanish conquistador Pedro Cieza de León first recorded it in 1549. Radiocarbon dating places its founding around AD 110, and the city grew significantly from about AD 375 to 700 on a complex agropastoral economy supported by trade. Its Southern Andean iconographic style is shared with the [[Wari culture]]. The society appears to have collapsed around AD 1000, and drought likely played a role. Claims of an age of 11,000 to 17,000 years, made by Arthur Posnansky from 1910 to 1945, are now rejected.

1960 Southern Gothic novel by Harper Lee. Loosely based on events near Lee's hometown of Monroeville, [[Alabama]], in 1936, it is narrated by Scout Finch as her lawyer father, Atticus Finch, defends a Black man falsely accused of raping a white woman. Its themes include racial injustice and the loss of innocence, and it won the [[Pulitzer Prize]] a year after publication. Atticus Finch has served as a moral hero for many readers and a model of integrity for lawyers. The 1962 film adaptation, starring [[Gregory Peck]], won three [[Academy Awards]]. Widely read in [[United States]] high schools and middle schools, the novel has nonetheless faced campaigns for removal from classrooms over its racial epithets. It remained Lee's only published book until *Go Set a Watchman*, an earlier draft, appeared in 2015.

1927 novel by [[Virginia Woolf]]. Set on the Isle of Skye in Scotland, it follows the Ramsay family's visits between 1910 and 1920 to their summer house. Extending the modernism of [[Marcel Proust]] and [[James Joyce]], it has little dialogue and almost no direct action, with the plot secondary to philosophical introspection. It is cited as a key example of multiple focalization and is told in three parts: The Window, Time Passes and The Lighthouse. Its themes include loss, subjectivity, the nature of art and the problem of perception. The Modern Library ranked it No. 15 among the 100 best English-language novels of the 20th century in 1998, and *[[Time (magazine)|Time]]* included it in its 2005 list of the 100 best English-language novels since 1923.

Product prepared from the cured leaves of [[Plant|plants]] of the genus *Nicotiana*. The chief commercial crop is *Nicotiana tabacum*. Dried leaves are used mainly for smoking in [[Cigarette|cigarettes]], cigars, pipes and hookahs, and also as snuff and chewing tobacco. Tobacco contains the addictive stimulant alkaloid [[Nicotine|nicotine]], making it among the most widely used recreational drugs. Its use causes or raises the risk of many deadly diseases, especially those of the [[Heart|heart]], liver and [[Lung|lungs]], and of many cancers. In 2008 the [[World Health Organization]] named tobacco use the world's single greatest preventable cause of death. The word derives from Spanish *tabaco*, probably from the Taíno language of the Caribbean. Tobacco was used ceremonially in the Americas for thousands of years, with some cultivation in Mexico dating to 1400–1000 BCE. After European contact it spread worldwide, and the English colony of [[Jamestown]] used it as currency and an export crop. Its demand was closely tied to [[Slavery]] in the Caribbean.

RNA [[Virus|virus]] that infects many plants, especially [[Tobacco|tobacco]]. It causes mottled, mosaic-like discoloration of the leaves and was the first virus discovered. Adolf Mayer described the disease in 1886. In 1892 Dmitri Ivanovsky showed that its infectious agent passed through filters fine enough to trap [[Bacteria|bacteria]]. In 1898 Martinus Beijerinck showed that it reproduces in host cells and adopted the term virus. Wendell Meredith Stanley crystallized it in 1935, news that appeared on the front page of *[[The New York Times]]*. Stanley received one-fourth of the 1946 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, although some of his conclusions were later shown to be incorrect. [[Rosalind Franklin]] built a model of the virus for the 1958 World's Fair in [[Brussels]]. Its rod-shaped capsid is made of 2,130 coat-protein molecules around a single 6,400-base RNA strand.

Practice of burning [[Tobacco|tobacco]] and absorbing the smoke into the body. Smoking is the most common way to consume tobacco. The practice is believed to have begun as early as 5000–3000 BC in [[Mesoamerica]] and [[South America]], and it reached [[Eurasia]] in the 17th century through European colonists. Nicotine, the addictive psychostimulant in smoke, is absorbed through the lungs or the oral mucosa, and [[Dopamine|dopamine]] is released, leading to [[Addiction|addiction]]. German scientists linked smoking to lung cancer in the late 1920s, and British researchers demonstrated a clear relationship with cancer in 1950. Consumption in the developed world has peaked or declined since 1965, but it continues to climb in the developing world. The [[World Health Organization]] attributes 8 million deaths a year to tobacco smoking. Many smokers begin in [[Adolescence|adolescence]], often influenced by cigarette advertising, parents, siblings and friends.

Historical [[Indo-European languages|Indo-European]]-speaking people of the Tarim Basin, in present-day [[Xinjiang]], China. They spoke the Tocharian languages, known from about 7,600 documents from the 6th and 7th centuries. Early 20th-century scholars linked their speakers to the Tókharoi of [[Bactria]], an identification now considered erroneous. Agricultural communities appeared in the northern Tarim oases around 2000 BC and developed into city-states by the 2nd century BC, the largest being Kucha. These served as way stations on the [[Silk Road]] along the northern edge of the Taklamakan Desert. The basin was then ruled by the [[Xiongnu]], the [[Han dynasty]], the Tibetan Empire and the [[Tang dynasty]]. From the 8th century AD the Turkic-speaking [[Uyghurs]] settled in the region. The Tocharian languages are believed to have become extinct in the 9th century. Their origins are uncertain, with proposed links to the Andronovo and Afanasievo cultures.

Soy-based food made by pressing the curds of coagulated [[Soy milk|soy milk]] into solid white blocks. Tofu originated in [[China]] and has been eaten for over 2,000 years. It is a traditional component of East and Southeast Asian cuisines, and Western cooking commonly uses it as a meat substitute. Blocks range from silken and soft to firm and extra firm. Tofu making was first recorded in the [[Han dynasty]], and legend credits Prince Liu An (179–122 BC) with its invention. It did not become popular in China until the [[Song dynasty]] (960–1279). It spread with [[Buddhism|Buddhism]], which made it an important protein source in East Asian vegetarian diets, and tofu first appears in [[Japan|Japanese]] records in AD 965. Tofu is low in calories but rich in protein. [[Soybean|Soybean]] cultivation needs little land (1.3 m² per 1,000 kcal) and emits little greenhouse gas per gram of protein (1.6 kg CO₂ per 100 g of protein).

Country in West Africa. Officially the Togolese Republic, Togo is bordered by [[Ghana]] to the west, [[Benin]] to the east and [[Burkina Faso]] to the north. It is one of the least developed countries, with a lower-middle-income economy that depends mostly on agriculture and [[Phosphate|phosphate]] mining. The coast served as a European slave-trading outpost from the 16th to the 18th centuries. In 1884, during the [[Scramble for Africa]], Germany established a protectorate known as Togoland, which passed to France after [[World War I]]. Togo became independent in 1960. Gnassingbé Eyadéma seized power in a 1967 coup and was president for 38 years, until his death; his son Faure Gnassingbé was elected president in 2005. French is the official language, and about half the population is Christian, with Muslims and adherents of traditional religions also present. Togo is a member of the [[United Nations]] and the [[African Union]].

Japanese film production, distribution and theater company, based in [[Tokyo]]. Founded in 1932 as the Tokyo-Takarazuka Theatre Company, Toho is best known for producing [[Kaiju|kaiju]] films, including [[Godzilla]], which appears in 36 of its films, and the films of [[Akira Kurosawa]]. It has also distributed animated films from [[Studio Ghibli]]. Its [[Doraemon]] series, distributed since 1980, is the highest-grossing film series in Japan. Toho is the largest of Japan's Big Four film studios and the only film studio in the Nikkei 225 index.

Sanitary hardware that collects human urine and feces, usually for disposal. Flush toilets use water and are usually connected to a sewer system in urban areas or a septic tank in isolated areas, while dry toilets use no water. Sitting toilets are popular in Europe and North America, while squatting toilets are more popular in [[Asia|Asia]]. Toilets are commonly made of [[Ceramic|ceramic]] (porcelain), concrete, plastic or wood, and Japan is known for its toilet technology. [[Sanitation|Sanitation]] has concerned [[Human settlement|human settlements]] since their earliest stages. Poor sanitation spreads diseases through the fecal-oral route, including [[Cholera]] and [[Dysentery]]. An estimated 419 million people have no toilet at all and must defecate in the open, a problem addressed by UN Sustainable Development Goal 6.

Dependent territory of [[New Zealand]] in the [[Pacific Ocean|South Pacific Ocean]]. It consists of three tropical coral [[Atoll|atolls]], with a combined land area of 10 sq km and about 2,500 people. It has the smallest economy of any nation, yet it is the first 100% solar-powered nation in the world and a leader in [[Renewable energy|renewable energy]]. New Zealand and the Tokelauan government both officially call it a nation. In 2007 the UN General Assembly listed it as non-self-governing, but Tokelauans have twice narrowly failed to reach a two-thirds majority in [[Self-determination|self-determination]] referendums.

Mongol khan of the [[Golden Horde]]. He belonged to the House of Borjigin, tracing his ancestry to [[Genghis Khan]]. After years as a fugitive, during which he sought help from the Turco-Mongol warlord [[Timur]], he consolidated power in both wings of the Golden Horde and briefly unified the Blue and White Hordes into a single polity. In 1382 he besieged and sacked [[Moscow]], reasserting Tatar–Mongol hegemony over the [[Russia|Russian]] principalities and restoring tribute payments. His former protector Timur later invaded the Golden Horde and defeated him twice, undoing his achievements. Tokhtamysh is often called the last great ruler of the Golden Horde.

Japanese samurai and daimyo, founder and first [[Shogun|shogun]] of the [[Tokugawa shogunate]]. Born Matsudaira Takechiyo, he was one of the three Great Unifiers of Japan, along with [[Oda Nobunaga]] and [[Toyotomi Hideyoshi]]. After Hideyoshi's death and Ieyasu's victory at the [[Battle of Sekigahara]] in 1600, he seized power. He was appointed shogun in 1603 and resigned in 1605, but retained de facto control of government until his death. He built his castle at Edo, now [[Tokyo]], and implemented the bakuhan system, which used graded rewards and punishments to keep the daimyo and samurai at peace. His successors enacted the sakoku policy of isolation in 1639, closing Japan off from most outside contact for over 200 years, with some exceptions.

Military government of Japan during the [[Edo period]], 1603–1868. Founded by [[Tokugawa Ieyasu]] after his victory at the [[Battle of Sekigahara]] in 1600, it ended the civil wars of the [[Sengoku period]]. The Tokugawa governed from Edo Castle in Edo, now Tokyo, together with daimyo lords who each administered a han, or feudal domain. Society was organized into a strict class system of samurai, farmers, artisans and merchants. Daimyo were required to keep their wives and children in the capital as hostages. Under the isolationist sakoku policy, most foreigners were barred and Japanese subjects could not leave the country. Growth and urbanization fostered a merchant class and ukiyo culture. The shogunate declined from 1853 and was overthrown in the [[Meiji Restoration]] of 1868; loyalists continued the [[Boshin War]] until 1869.

1953 Japanese drama film by [[Yasujirō Ozu]]. Chishū Ryū and Chieko Higashiyama play an aging couple from Onomichi who travel to [[Tokyo]] to visit their grown children. The children are too busy to entertain them, and only their widowed daughter-in-law, Noriko, played by [[Setsuko Hara]], makes time for them. Japanese film exporters initially considered it too Japanese to be marketable abroad, but it won the inaugural Sutherland Trophy in London in 1958. Critics regard it as Ozu's magnum opus. It portrays postwar Japanese family life and the growing distance between parents and children. In the 2012 *Sight and Sound* poll of film experts, it was voted the third-greatest film of all time.

Terrorist attack by the [[Aum Shinrikyo]] cult in 1995. On March 20, 1995, members of Aum Shinrikyo released the nerve agent sarin on three [[Tokyo]] Metro lines during rush hour, in five coordinated attacks. Fourteen people were killed, about 50 were severely injured and nearly 1,000 had temporary vision problems. Police raids followed, and more than 200 members were arrested. Thirteen senior members, including Shoko Asahara, were sentenced to death and later executed. The attack remains the deadliest modern terrorist incident in Japan.

City (pop., 2020: 270,871) in Ohio, United States, and county seat of Lucas County. Located at the western end of [[Lake Erie]] on the Maumee River, its port is the fifth-busiest on the [[Great Lakes]]. Founded in 1833, it grew after the 1845 completion of the Miami and Erie Canal and lay on the railway line between [[New York City]] and [[Chicago]]. It was nicknamed the Glass City after glass manufacturers arrived in the 1880s. After World War II it turned largely to automotive production, and its population has declined from its peak amid [[Rust Belt]] deindustrialization.
